nodes.what: A local-first review press: combine a static, keyboard-accessible diff and anchored comments with the exact Git bundle under review, so occasional reviewers can inspect, annotate and return one portable packet without a forge, daemon or account.
nodes.why: Git bundles already move commits without a server; Gerrit NoteDb and Radicle prove review metadata can live in Git and support offline work. The proposed missing value is deliberately narrower than another forge or P2P network: one self-contained, human-auditable packet for an occasional reviewer with no daemon/account/key setup, combining a static accessible diff, line comments/resolution, explicit review evidence, and the matching Git bundle. This could serve air-gapped teams, classroom reviews, volunteers exchanging drives, or maintainers archiving reasoning beside a release. It is a weeks-long candidate because safe diff/anchor handling, concurrent review merge, accessible UI, bundle compatibility and independent two-person trials are separate milestones. Uncertainty: Radicle already offers offline patches with signed identities and Gerrit has mature patch sets, so this should lose unless the zero-service packet workflow proves simpler in actual use. Authentication is out of scope: hashes bind bytes, never prove who wrote a comment. No demand or adoption is established.
nodes.first_step: After selection, build only projects/review-skein/ milestone 1: a stdlib CLI that reads two named committed refs in a real Git fixture repo and writes a versioned review packet containing immutable base/head IDs, a static escaped side-by-side diff, and an ordinary full Git bundle; reject uncommitted or ambiguous refs, unsafe paths, binaries and oversized files honestly. Add a small comment model anchored to commit/path/old-or-new line with an explicit orphan-on-rebase state, JSON roundtrip and tests for renamed files, Unicode, tabs, duplicate lines, missing anchors and bundle verification/reproduction. A non-author exports a packet from one fixture, opens it without network and records one comment before later milestones add merging. No authentication, merge/apply or live service in the first milestone.

nodes.title: Chorus: an oral-history box with consent in the package
nodes.what: A private, local-first studio for families and small history groups: preserve original recordings, attach consent and timecoded chapters, then export a playable static archive whose media and transcript share permissions are inspectable and travel together.
nodes.why: StoryCorps already guides recording, private drafts and audio export; OHMS already links timecoded transcripts/indexes to hosted media and exports XML. The proposed gap is not recording or transcription generally: a completely local interview box whose share decision travels with each original media file and transcript segment, producing a playable static archive that a family or small museum can keep, copy and inspect without installing a viewer or putting media on a server. Consent records are documentation, not a legal-compliance guarantee; originals stay unchanged and withheld material is omitted from share exports while remaining marked in the private project. Weeks-long scope: robust media import, timecoded chapter editing, private/share export boundaries, offline accessible playback/search, optional recording, and independent field/preservation trials. Uncertainty: browser storage limits and long interviews may require a filesystem-backed shell; manual timecoding is labor; no claim that families will prefer it to StoryCorps or that OHMS cannot meet archival needs. Outside demand is plausible, not measured.
nodes.first_step: After selection, build only projects/chorus-archive/ milestone 1: import one small user-supplied WAV with title, participants, a consent note and several manually timecoded transcript chapters; keep the original unchanged. Export a deterministic private project plus a share folder containing static HTML, copied permitted media, WebVTT/JSON/plain transcript, per-file SHA-256 manifest, and a non-sensitive omissions inventory. Any narrator/session lacking an explicit share flag, and every restricted segment, must be absent from the share payload rather than merely hidden in its UI. Tests cover HTML escaping, unsafe paths, invalid/overlapping timestamps, duplicate IDs, missing/changed media, whole-interview withholding and import/export roundtrip. A non-author opens the result without network, plays a supplied fixture, checks keyboard transcript navigation and verifies restricted bytes are absent. No automatic transcription, preservation-quality claim or legal-compliance claim.

nodes.title: Skein: a code review you can carry across an air gap
nodes.what: A local-first review press: combine a static, keyboard-accessible diff and anchored comments with the exact Git bundle under review, so occasional reviewers can inspect, annotate and return one portable packet without a forge, daemon or account.
nodes.why: Git bundles already move commits without a server; Gerrit NoteDb and Radicle prove review metadata can live in Git and support offline work. The proposed missing value is deliberately narrower than another forge or P2P network: one self-contained, human-auditable packet for an occasional reviewer with no daemon/account/key setup, combining a static accessible diff, line comments/resolution, explicit review evidence, and the matching Git bundle. This could serve air-gapped teams, classroom reviews, volunteers exchanging drives, or maintainers archiving reasoning beside a release. It is a weeks-long candidate because safe diff/anchor handling, concurrent review merge, accessible UI, bundle compatibility and independent two-person trials are separate milestones. Uncertainty: Radicle already offers offline patches with signed identities and Gerrit has mature patch sets, so this should lose unless the zero-service packet workflow proves simpler in actual use. Authentication is out of scope: hashes bind bytes, never prove who wrote a comment. No demand or adoption is established.
nodes.first_step: After selection, build only projects/review-skein/ milestone 1: a stdlib CLI that reads two named committed refs in a real Git fixture repo and writes a versioned review packet containing immutable base/head IDs, a static escaped side-by-side diff, and an ordinary full Git bundle; reject uncommitted or ambiguous refs, unsafe paths, binaries and oversized files honestly. Add a small comment model anchored to commit/path/old-or-new line with an explicit orphan-on-rebase state, JSON roundtrip and tests for renamed files, Unicode, tabs, duplicate lines, missing anchors and bundle verification/reproduction. A non-author exports a packet from one fixture, opens it without network and records one comment before later milestones add merging. No authentication, merge/apply or live service in the first milestone.

nodes.title: Chorus: an oral-history box with consent in the package
nodes.what: A private, local-first studio for families and small history groups: preserve original recordings, attach consent and timecoded chapters, then export a playable static archive whose media and transcript share permissions are inspectable and travel together.
nodes.why: StoryCorps already guides recording, private drafts and audio export; OHMS already links timecoded transcripts/indexes to hosted media and exports XML. The proposed gap is not recording or transcription generally: a completely local interview box whose share decision travels with each original media file and transcript segment, producing a playable static archive that a family or small museum can keep, copy and inspect without installing a viewer or putting media on a server. Consent records are documentation, not a legal-compliance guarantee; originals stay unchanged and withheld material is omitted from share exports while remaining marked in the private project. Weeks-long scope: robust media import, timecoded chapter editing, private/share export boundaries, offline accessible playback/search, optional recording, and independent field/preservation trials. Uncertainty: browser storage limits and long interviews may require a filesystem-backed shell; manual timecoding is labor; no claim that families will prefer it to StoryCorps or that OHMS cannot meet archival needs. Outside demand is plausible, not measured.
